lesson_title: The Drawing That Speaks Builder: Plans, Elevations and Packing
hook_text: An architect's plan is secret code with only ten words. Learn them before your tea gets cold.
clip_script: Your cousin unrolls the plan of her new house and it looks like secret writing. It is — but the language has ten words. Fat double lines: walls, and the gap between them is the wall's real thickness. A gap with a little quarter-moon: a door, and the moon shows which way it swings — so no bed can stand behind it. Thin double lines: a window. WC: the toilet. Now the magic number: 1 to 100 — every centimetre of paper is a METRE of house. Ruler on the bedroom: 45 by 30 millimetres. Real room: 4,5 by 3 metres. Will the 2-metre wardrobe fit? Draw a 20-millimetre rectangle and park it — you just moved furniture with a pencil instead of your back. But the floor plan has a blind spot: UP. It cannot see heights. For that, walk around the paper house — the elevations stare at each wall like a neighbour: window heights, roof, doors. One trap: step outside the north wall and left becomes right, like a friend's raised right hand facing your left. Anchor to the compass — west never flips. Then to the hardware store: 150 tiles plus ten percent is 165, boxes of twelve, buy FOURTEEN. Shops sell whole boxes — and the maths always rounds up.
visual_style: A rolled plan opening across a kitchen table, symbols lighting up one by one with labels; a pencil wardrobe sliding around a plan room; the flat drawing folding up into a 3D house as elevations snap onto each wall; a stack of tile boxes counting to 14.
pacing: Rapid symbol tour, a pause on the centimetre-is-a-metre reveal, playful wardrobe slide, crisp rounding-up finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any plan, match any elevation, and buy exactly enough tiles and paint.
